top.line: I want to buy one HBR article, not subscribe
top.para: Following a LinkedIn link to an HBR article, I was offered subscriptions from £11 a month to £105 a year, or a $11.95 reprint. A month's plan across September's 45 articles works out at 24p to 55p each. Beyond the article, the graph, vocabulary, evidence, briefings and a licence to quote are all billable units.

in-short.line: A fair price is pennies; only subscriptions are sold
in-short.para: I wanted to pay HBR for one article and was offered a subscription, though the arithmetic says 24p to 55p and the reprint is $11.95, priced for a team. The graph, vocabulary, evidence, briefings and licence to quote are each billable, and most run on this newsroom. LinkedIn readers are a market, not a leak.

what-happened.line: Every option offered was a subscription, none the article
what-happened.para: Clicking through from Olivier Laplace's LinkedIn post, I met a modal and three plans: Digital at £8.75 or £11, Digital & Print at £10 or £13, Premium at £15 or £18. The only other door was a $11.95 reprint, $9.75 for five to ten. I want to pay HBR, but not subscribe.

arithmetic.line: One article should cost between 25p and a pound
arithmetic.para: HBR.org's feed lists 45 articles in September 2026. At £11 a month that is about 24p an article if I read all of them, 55p for twenty, £1.10 for ten. A fair single-article price is 25p to a pound, yet I am asked £11 or $11.95: ten to forty-five times what I want.

here.line: Here readers pay pennies after reading, set by usefulness
here.para: Since 11 October this newsroom has taken real payments: 10p for a new article, 5p for an older one, charged for the share read, after reading, from a balance in the reader's browser. Nothing is blocked, the reader's rating sets the price from nothing to double, and a faulty page costs nothing.

units.line: LinkedIn readers need many things HBR could sell
units.para: Beyond the article, HBR could sell my own reading record and personas, its argument as a graph, its editor-verified vocabulary, the evidence as a graph priced by step, versions for a CFO, CISO or board, a licence to quote with a revenue share, a check of my use, and next steps. Most already run here.

loop.line: LinkedIn is HBR's best market, not a leak
loop.para: HBR's modal treats LinkedIn as a leak, but the executives, consultants and founders discussing its articles there are the readers it wants. The only way to pay is to subscribe, so most read and move on. Olivier's post, with fifty reactions and twenty-one comments, is a room HBR cannot sell to.

ask.line: Sell the article, its graph, and licences to quote
ask.para: HBR has content, brand and readers but no way for most to pay. Sell the article for pennies to a pound after reading, sell the graph, vocabulary, evidence and versions, license quotes with a share, let readers keep their reading in their own vault, and treat LinkedIn as a storefront. It already runs on newsroom.sgit.ai.

limits.line: UK prices on one day, small numbers, a stake
limits.para: HBR's prices are as shown to a UK reader on 17 October 2026, and the 45 is a lower bound. This newsroom has few readers, so it shows the model works, not that it scales. The licence to quote and the use check are proposals, and I build this newsroom's reader code.

sources.line: Sources: HBR's pages, a LinkedIn post and site articles
sources.para: A voice memo of mine from 17 October 2026, written up by the site's agent. HBR's article page, subscription offer, store reprint price and feed, all read that day; Olivier Laplace's LinkedIn post; and this newsroom's pages for publishers, the reading meter, the reader API, Pay after you read and many related articles.
